title: Metabolic control of human endothelial development via the COUP-TF/1-deoxysphingosine axis
text:
The vascular and lymphatic systems are essential for delivering oxygen and nutrients to organs, removing waste
products and regulating tissue fluid homeostasis and immune cell trafficking. We propose to define the role of
nuclear hormone receptor NR2F1/2 in the specification of arterial, venous and lymphatic endothelium, reveal the
molecular mechanisms that regulate ligand-dependent NR2F1/2 transcription and provide a structural basis for
designing synthetic agonists/ antagonists to modulate NR2F1/2 activity. The proposed research is relevant to
public health because a thorough understanding of transcriptional networks driving endothelial development is
critical for designing regenerative treatments to repair blood and lymphatic vessels damaged by congenital
conditions or disease. Thus, the proposed research is relevant to the part of NIH’s mission that pertains to
developing of fundamental knowledge that will help reduce the burdens of illness and disability.

title: Modeling Normal and Abnormal Trophoblasts
text: Preeclampsia is the leading cause of maternal mortality worldwide. The proposed project will utilize three recently developed, highly innovative cell culture models to understand how the development of the placenta is disrupted in preeclampsia.

title: FcγRIIa-induced Activation of Platelet αIIbβ3 in Thrombosis and Thromboinflammation
text:
Platelet interactions with fibrinogen, fibrin, and von Willebrand factor contribute to abnormal clotting in heart
attacks, stroke, and inflammatory conditions, such as COVID-19. Past studies from this grant produced the
drug abciximab to treat patients with heart attacks; tests to monitor the effects of antiplatelet drugs like
clopidogrel (Plavix); and a new drug for heart attacks (RUC-4, zalunfiban) that is undergoing human testing.
Our new studies are designed to develop a deeper understanding of the receptor that the platelet uses to bind
these proteins, αIIbβ3, and the receptor that results in platelet activation by immune complexes, FcγRIIa, using
new sophisticated methods, with the goal of developing even better therapies for heart attacks, strokes, and
immunothrombosis.

title: Interrogating microglia-driven retinal ganglion cell and vascular dysfunction in metabolic syndrome associated retinopathy
text:
Retinal vascular diseases, including diabetic retinopathy (DR), are a leading cause of vision loss worldwide.
Beyond vascular dysfunction, DR is linked to neuronal and immune cell abnormalities. In this application, my
goal is to identify mechanisms by which retinal immune cells contribute to the progression of a DR-like metabolic
syndrome associated retinopathy, including the accumulation of vascular and neuronal damage, using new
mouse models.

title: Elucidating kinetics and thermodynamics of RNA-ligand interactions using single molecule approaches
text:
RNA folds into secondary and tertiary structures critical to biological function in gene regulation, viral replication
and other critical processes whose disruption can mitigate or promote disease. Here, I outline a proposed
implementation of biophysical single molecule measurements and analysis tools to quantify the structural and
energetic features of biologically important RNAs in order to develop the mechanistic understanding necessary
for therapeutic intervention and drug development against RNA targets.

title: Neuroimaging Core - Cleveland ADRC
text: The Neuroimaging Core (NIC) has played a critical role in the Cleveland Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center’s (CADRC) ability to provide deep phenotyping and neuroimaging characterization of its participants. The NIC supports the acquisition of prospectively collected advanced imaging data and offers high-level analysis capabilities and infrastructure to CADRC cores, as well as to Alzheimer’s Disease and Alzheimer’s Disease related dementias (AD/ADRD) researchers regionally and nationally. The core also contributes standardized benchmark imaging data (e.g., structural MRI and amyloid and tau PET) to the National Alzheimer’s Coordinating Center (NACC). Led by Drs. Mark Lowe and Frank DiFilippo, the NIC benefits from decades of expertise in developing advanced imaging techniques and continues to build on the strengths of Northeast Ohio’s cutting- edge imaging technology ecosystem. In the next grant cycle, the NIC will continue to support CADRC imaging acquisition and data dissemination (Aim 1). It will expand its role in investigating factors related to the rate of disease progression, an aim that is central to both the CADRC theme and national priorities outlined in the NAPA goals. Towards this the NIC will provide longitudinal quantitative imaging biomarkers to facilitate deep phenotyping of participants and enable personalized research insights (Aim 2). In collaboration with the Neuropathology Core, the NIC will acquire ultrahigh-resolution 7T MRI scans of ex vivo brain hemispheres from brain donors to further enhance postmortem imaging-pathology correlations (Aim 3). Additionally, the NIC will provide access to state-of-the-art imaging modalities such as microstructure MRI (µMRI), quantitative cerebral blood flow (CBF), dynamic contrast-enhanced imaging (DCE), and MR fingerprinting (MRF) to support a wide range of AD/ADRD research. A central mission of the NIC is to train and mentor new and early-career investigators, including REC Scholars, in the application of neuroimaging to AD/ADRD research (Aim 4).

title: Genetic dissection of the 17q21.31 MAPT locus in neurodegenerative disease
text:
The 17q21.31 locus is one of the most genetically complex loci in the human genome and its strong
association with multiple neurodegenerative diseases including Alzheimer’s disease mark it as a critical
modifier of disease risk. In addition to the microtubule-associated protein tau (MAPT) gene, this locus harbors
more than a dozen other genes whose contribution to neurological diseases remains largely unexplored. Here,
we propose to use statistical genetics, machine learning, and functional genomics to uncover the genes that
drive disease risk, thus nominating pathways and cell types that will inform future mechanistic studies and
inspire therapeutic approaches.

title: Mito-inflammation and sepsis-induced acute lung injury
text:
NARRATIVE/RELEVANCE:
Despite recent advances in the care of the critically ill, there remains a need for an improved understanding of
the pathophysiology of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Improved therapeutic options are also
needed. We propose to investigate new therapeutic approaches targeting mitochondrial network dynamics,
which will result in the development of precise, individualized therapies for the critically ill.

title: Interspecies microbial interactions in CKD
text:
Chronic kidney disease is a gradual loss of kidney function, which is a major cause of morbidity
and mortality in the US. Once kidney damage occurs, it results in incomplete removal of toxic
products made by our microflora, termed uremic toxins, which accelerates disease progression.
Chronic kidney disease is linked to changes in the composition of our microflora (dysbiosis), but
it remains unclear whether these compositional changes accelerate disease progression.
Successful completion of the proposed research will reveal the ecological causes of dysbiosis
and determine whether dysbiosis has causative effects on chronic kidney disease progression.
This information will be a critical first step for translating advances in microbiome research into
clinical intervention.

title: Plasticity of Type 3 Innate Lymphoid Cells Regulated by Intestinal Microenvironment
text:
(2-3 sentences):
Under conditions of acute or chronic inflammation caused by infections or various inflammatory diseases
including inflammatory bowel diseases, many immune cell subtypes are activated and may expand or become
dysregulated, thereby contributing the pathogenic tissue damage. Although plasticity in immune cells like T cells
and innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) affords these cells the flexibility to facilitate both tissue inflammation and repair
based on the context-dependent regulation of T cell and ILC functions, the underlying mechanisms governing
the plasticity of ILCs have not yet been well characterized. In this proposal, we plan to investigate the mechanistic
basis for the transdifferentiation of ILCs in response to infection, acute inflammation, or chronic gut inflammation
with a specific focus on the roles that these plastic ILCs play in vivo and on the conversion between ILC2s and
ILC3s such that these results may offer new insight into how best to control ILC responses under conditions of
ILC2- or ILC3-intensive tissue inflammation such as IBD.

title: AI-enabled characterization of fibrocalcific aortic valve disease and inflammation from CT Angiography: Patient-specific outcome prediction
text:
In patients with aortic stenosis (the most common heart valve disease), imaging of the heart and aorta with
Computed Tomography Angiography (CTA) allows doctors to noninvasively assess the aortic valve. The
researchers propose to accurately characterize aortic stenosis by novel computerized measurements of fibrotic
and calcific components of aortic valves, as well as their progression over time. They propose to further develop
and validate new computerized risk scores, derived from these CTA measurements and clinical patient data
using artificial intelligence, that will automatically identify the patient’s risk of suffering death or stroke, following
minimally invasive transcatheter aortic valve replacement.

title: Digital Sleep Intervention for Families of Young Children
text:
This grant will support my career goal of becoming an independent scientist with expertise in developing,
testing, implementing and scaling accessible, engaging, family-centered preventive interventions. Specifically, I
plan to focus on digitally enabled interventions tailored for Black families of young children with sleep problems
as a promising strategy to promote sleep health at the population level. I will develop and pilot test the
intervention, and use findings, to optimize the intervention and design a randomized controlled trial to evaluate
implementation and effectiveness outcomes.

title: Reprogramming myogenic regulatory factors in RMS to promote differentiation and halt growth
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because understanding the
mechanism of Embryonal Rhabdomyosarcoma progression is expected to deepen our
understanding of how developmental transcription factors are reactivated in disease, and
to provide evidence that targeting these developmental genes (which are no longer
required in most differentiated cells) may be a novel means to inhibit RMS without the
associated toxicities of most therapies. Such toxicities can be particularly devastating to
children, and thus novel therapies, developed through the generation of unique animal
models such as human xenograft into mice and zebrafish models, are clearly needed to
identify new means to treat the disease. Thus, the proposed research is relevant to the
NCI mission that pertains to advancing scientific knowledge and helping all people
to live longer, healthier lives.

title: Noncoding RNAs in gamma-Herpesvirus Biology and AIDS Malignancies
text:
The unifying postulate of this competitive renewal P01 proposal is that comparative studies of KSHV, EBV, and
MHV68 will continue to accelerate the discovery of pathways regulated by non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs). Our
findings over the last 4 years indicate that both short and long ncRNAs contribute to γ-herpesvirus latency and
tumorigenesis.

title: Modulation of YAP/TAZ Signaling for the Prevention and Therapy of Cardiovascular Disease
text:
Atherosclerosis, the leading cause of heart attacks and strokes, is driven in part by abnormal
movement of vascular smooth muscle cells within blood vessels. This project will test whether a
new drug, IAG933, can restore healthy cell adhesion and prevent harmful cell migration by
blocking a key signaling pathway. The findings may lead to new therapies to reduce
cardiovascular disease while also providing research training opportunities for undergraduate
students in biomedical science.

title: A Human Gut-Liver Platform with Microbiome Interactions for In Vitro Toxicology
text:
The intestine and the liver are anatomically and physiologically connected, referred to as the gut-liver axis,
which also plays a key role in the pathogenesis of several liver diseases. Here, scalable human gut-liver models
containing primary cells will be developed for in vitro applications, such as compound screening and disease
modeling, and be used to elucidate the effects of reciprocal tissue crosstalk on cell phenotype modulation.

title: Core 1: Information Technology and Systems Integration
text:
The IT and Systems Integrations Core will manage and support the data and bioinformatics infrastructure needs of the
four projects. Specific aims include support for return of results at point of care, collection and processing of electronic
patient reported outcomes (ePRO), and integration of pathology and biomarker data as source classifiers. The core team is
deeply integrated into the I-SPY2.2 trial and will continually receive requirements and feedback to enhance IT platforms
ensuring the Project needs are met.

title: Understanding and targeting the DNA replication stress in cancer cells
text:
DNA replication problems collectively known as replication stress are a major source of genomic instability in
cancer cells and also a vulnerability of cancer that can be exploited therapeutically. We will systematically define
and characterize different types of replication stress and the resulting vulnerabilities, investigate the impacts of
RNA on DNA replication and repair, and explore the cell non-autonomous effects of replication stress, building
a new molecular basis for exploiting replication stress in cancer therapy.

title: Hemogenetic imaging technology for circuit-specific analysis of primate brain function
text:
The cognitive capabilities of primates depend on integrated interactions among cells and brain areas that cur-
rently cannot be studied at a whole-brain level in live animals. In this project, we will adapt and validate a un-
precedented experimental approach called hemogenetic imaging, which permits brain-wide functional measure-
ments from genetically targeted cell types and circuit elements. Through technology development and multi-
laboratory collaboration, this project will establish transformative and broadly applicable methodology for inves-
tigation of primate brain function.

title: Deep Learning-based Diagnosis of Retinopathy of Prematurity
text:
Deep learning-based diagnosis would provide a consistent diagnosis of retinopathy of prematurity (ROP),
especially plus disease, and may improve clinical access to the underserved region via telemedicine. However,
the performance of deep learning-based diagnosis is hindered by limited data availability in the training phase of
the model and the image quality variations due to different acquisition systems. This study aims to develop a
deep learning technology to augment the training dataset using animal-to-human translated images and
standardize the image quality for images acquired cross-platforms using multi-task learning.
